title: Better Than the Photos

title: The First Time I Saw the Sea
paragraphs: I was nine when I first saw the sea. We had driven five hours and I had asked, how much longer, at least twenty times.

We stayed two hours. I did not swim much. Mostly I stood at the edge and let the water come to my feet and go back.
On the way home I fell asleep at once. My father says I talked about waves in my sleep for half the journey.

title: Why Old Towns Look Alike
paragraphs: Visit three old towns in three provinces and you will start to feel you have been to the same one.

So when you go, look for the parts nobody photographed: a wall with different bricks, or a door with two kinds of paint.

title: The Museum Nobody Visits
paragraphs: Every city has a famous museum with a queue, and a quiet one with a guard asleep at the door.

So put one small museum on your list. It will not be the photo you show people, but it will be the hour you remember.

title: Saying Yes and Saying No
paragraphs: When a friend invites you, there are three answers, not two: yes, no, and yes but not that day.

Being invited again next month matters more than attending this week.

title: How Do You Feel Today

title: Sleep Is Not a Luxury
paragraphs: Many students treat sleep as the thing you give up when there is too much to do. That is the wrong way round.

And you should not use a phone in bed. The screen keeps your brain awake for an hour after you put it down.
Eight hours is not a rule for weak people. It is what the body uses to turn work into memory.

title: Ten Thousand Steps

So do not count to ten thousand. Notice whether you sat down all day, and if you did, go out before dinner.

title: Why Breakfast Matters
paragraphs: Breakfast is not magic. It does not make you thinner or smarter. But skipping it changes how the morning goes.
After ten hours without food, your body has little energy ready. You can still work, but it costs more effort.
You do not need a big breakfast. Bread, an egg, and a glass of milk take four minutes and are enough.
If you have no time, the answer is to get up ten minutes earlier, not to skip the meal.

title: Sitting All Day

You should stand up every forty minutes, even for two minutes. Walk to the window, look far off, sit down again.
This is easier at school than at home, because school at least makes you walk between rooms.

title: Water

title: A Spending Plan
paragraphs: A spending plan is not a list of things you cannot buy. It is a decision made in advance so you do not decide in a shop.

The third part matters. A plan with no waste in it will break in the second week and you will blame the plan.
Review it once a month. Two minutes is enough, and it stops small leaks from becoming a hole.

title: Why Cheap Things Cost More

Divide the price by the number of uses and the answer is usually clear. A cheap thing used twice is the worst buy.

title: Lending Money to a Friend
paragraphs: Lending money to a friend is not a money problem. It is a friendship problem that happens to involve money.
Before you lend, decide one thing: can you afford to lose this amount and the friend? If not, lend less.
Say the date out loud. Not soon, not next week, but the fifteenth. A vague date is how friendships get damaged.
And if you are the one borrowing, pay back early. It costs nothing and it buys you something money cannot.

title: What Ads Do

title: Two Weeks Without Snacks

I wrote down every time I wanted something. In fourteen days there were nineteen entries, and eleven were after eight.
I still buy snacks. But now I know that most of my money was not going on hunger. It was going on being tired.

Knowing this did not end the wonder. It changed it. The sky became larger and stranger than the stories.
So looking up is not childish. It is the oldest habit humans have, and we still do it with better instruments.

title: The Moon Is Moving Away

Four centimetres sounds small, and it is. But it has been happening for four billion years.
One day, very far from now, a total solar eclipse will no longer be possible. The Moon will be too small in the sky.

title: What a Telescope Does

In a city the main problem is not the telescope but the light. You can see the Moon and a few planets, and not much else.
Take the same telescope twenty kilometres out of the city and the sky fills up. The instrument did not change. The darkness did.

That takes an enormous amount of energy, and most of it is spent lifting the fuel you have not burned yet.
It is also why reusing a rocket matters. A rocket thrown away after one flight is like a plane thrown away after one trip.

title: Where the Electricity Comes From

The grid has almost no storage. Supply must match demand every second, which is why engineers watch it like a heartbeat.
So the question is not whether you use electricity. It is what was burned, or not burned, to make it.

title: Turn It Off

title: Learning in a Museum

title: Why We Sing Together
paragraphs: People have sung together for thousands of years, and not only for entertainment.
When a group sings, everyone breathes at the same time. Slow songs slow the heart a little, and loud songs speed it up.
Singing also makes a group feel like one group. Soldiers, workers and students have all used it for this reason.
You do not need a good voice to join in. You need to be in the room, close enough to hear the people beside you.

title: Small Parties
paragraphs: A party of sixty people is mostly work. A party of six is mostly talk.

With sixty there are ten conversations, and you spend the evening moving between them without finishing any.
So when you want to be happy together, invite fewer people. The food can be simple and the chairs do not matter.

title: Saying Thank You Properly
paragraphs: Thank you is a small phrase, and most people say it too fast, in a voice that means nothing.
A proper thank you names the thing: thank you for waiting for me in the rain for twenty minutes.
It also says what changed: because of that, I did not miss the last bus home.
And it asks for nothing back. A thank you with a request inside it is not really a thank you.
Try it once this week, and watch the other person's face while you say it.

title: Why the Mooncake Is Round

So when a box arrives at your door, count the cakes before you count the days.

But the shape has not changed, because the shape is what people remember when they think of a festival.

title: Keeping a Tradition Alive

So if you want to keep something, do not put it in a museum. Cook it, sing it, and teach it to somebody small.

title: Paper Before Paper

title: The Four That Travelled
paragraphs: Compass, paper, printing and gunpowder are called the four great inventions of China.
All four left the country and changed other places more than they changed home.
Gunpowder became guns in Europe. The compass made long sea voyages possible. Paper and printing made books cheap enough to argue with.
The inventions were Chinese. The changes they caused were worldwide, and that is a strange and interesting fact.

title: The Compass at Sea
paragraphs: A compass needle points north because the earth itself is a great magnet.
Chinese sailors used a floating needle on water long before ships sailed across open ocean.
Before the compass, sailors followed the coast and the stars. In cloudy weather, they stopped.
With a compass they could cross water they could not see across, and the map of the world got bigger.
A needle in a bowl of water is a small thing. It moved the edge of the known world.

title: One Block, One Page
paragraphs: Woodblock printing works like this: you cut the characters backwards into a flat block of wood, ink it, and press paper on it.
One block prints one page, as many times as you like. A book of two hundred pages needs two hundred blocks.
It sounds slow, and it was, but it was faster and cheaper than copying by hand.
Moveable type came later. In China it was less useful, because written Chinese has thousands of characters and each one needs its own piece.

title: Gunpowder Went Far
paragraphs: Gunpowder was found by people looking for a medicine that would let them live forever.
Instead they got a powder that burns very fast and makes a great deal of gas. In a closed tube, that gas pushes.
Fireworks came first, then weapons. The knowledge moved west along trade routes and changed wars everywhere.
It is a good example of an invention that nobody planned. The inventors were wrong about what they had found.

title: Cai Lun and the Cheap Sheet
paragraphs: In 105, an official named Cai Lun brought the emperor a kind of paper made from tree bark, old cloth and fish nets.
The materials were the point. They were rubbish, and rubbish is cheap and everywhere.
Earlier paper had been made, but from better materials, so it cost too much to use for ordinary writing.
The court accepted the new paper, and within a hundred years it was used for letters, contracts and school books.

title: The Bicycle's Slow Start
paragraphs: The first bicycle had no pedals. You sat on it and pushed your feet against the ground, like a child on a toy.
Then someone put pedals on the front wheel, which made the wheel bigger and bigger until the rider sat two metres up.
The chain fixed that. Two wheels of the same size, a chain, and the risk of falling went down.
It took about eighty years to get from pushing to pedalling, and nobody wrote the plan down in advance.

title: A Machine That Saves Time
paragraphs: A washing machine does in one hour what took a person three hours with a board and a basin.
But it did not only save time. It changed who did the work, and how much water a family used.
Early machines were dangerous. Clothes went through rollers, and hands sometimes went with them.
The modern machine is safe, boring, and completely unnoticed. That is usually what success looks like.

title: The Invention Nobody Notices
paragraphs: A screw is a small, cheap, ordinary thing, and it holds most of the modern world together.
The idea is a slope wrapped around a cylinder. A long gentle slope lets you push something in with little force.
Screws are in your chair, your phone, your door and the plane you flew in last summer.
Nobody has ever said, what a wonderful screw. Inventions that work perfectly become invisible very quickly.

title: My Grandfather's Radio
paragraphs: My grandfather's radio is a wooden box the size of a shoebox, with a cloth over the speaker and two round knobs.
In 1978 it was the only way to hear news in his village. Twenty people sat in his room at eight o'clock.
You turned one knob for the station and one for the volume, and you turned them slowly, or you lost the signal.
It still works. Last week we found a station playing opera, and he sat down and listened for an hour without speaking.

title: Inventions That Failed Well
paragraphs: Some inventions succeed at something other than what they were made for.
A glue that was too weak to hold parts became the sticky note on your desk.
A medicine that did not cure anything became a drink that people still buy a hundred years later.
The lesson is not that failure is good. The lesson is that a failure has to be looked at carefully before it is thrown away.
Most failures are early, not wrong.

title: What We Might Invent Next
paragraphs: Every age thinks it has invented the important things already, and every age has been wrong.
The inventions that will matter in fifty years are probably being made now in small rooms by people nobody has heard of.
Some will be about energy, because everything else depends on it. Some will be about water, for the same reason.
And some will be small and dull, like the screw, and we will not notice them until they are everywhere.

title: Graduation Week
paragraphs: The last week of primary school has no lessons, only jobs. Clean the classroom, sign the shirts, take the photos.
On Monday we wrote our names on each other's white shirts, and by Friday no white was left.
On Thursday our teacher put the six years of class photos on the wall, one for each year, in a line.
We stood in front of them and found ourselves in each one, smaller and smaller, going back to the beginning.

title: A Letter to My Six-Year-Old Self
paragraphs: Dear me at six, this letter comes from twelve, which is the last year of primary school.
You are worried about the first day of school. You will cry at the gate, and then you will be fine by lunch.
The boy who sits beside you will be your friend for six years, and you will not know that today.
Do not worry about being the fastest reader. Worry more about the people sitting on your left and right.
